Brown et al., [“Language Models Are Few-Shot Learners”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165), *NeurIPS 2020*, §4 (“Measuring and Preventing Memorization of Benchmarks”) and Appendix C: a bug in the overlap filter left some benchmark contamination, retraining was judged infeasible because of cost, and the authors measured its effect instead.

notes.evidence_checked: Official PyTorch data-loading and CUDA semantics documentation read at multiprocess loading, pinning and asynchronous transfers. Murray et al. primary abstract read for pipeline design/bottlenecks. Overlap requires more than pinning alone.
notes.citation_and_locator: PyTorch, [`torch.utils.data` documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html), “Multi-process data loading” and “Memory Pinning”; Derek G. Murray et al., [“tf.data: A Machine Learning Data Processing Framework”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.12127), *Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment* 14(12) (2021), on input pipelines as a training bottleneck. Pinned (page-locked) host memory enables asynchronous transfers; overlap with computation also requires suitable stream scheduling and hardware, as described in PyTorch’s [CUDA semantics](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html). Whether a job is input-bound depends on its data, preprocessing and hardware.

notes.evidence_checked: PyTorch CUDA semantics (asynchronous execution, streams, graphs) and Alan Gray’s NVIDIA CUDA-graphs article read, including its V100 timing example rather than generated summary. Ansel et al. primary PyTorch 2 paper checked at dynamic bytecode/graph compilation; graph breaks and device dependence are not universalized.
notes.citation_and_locator: PyTorch, [“CUDA semantics”](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html), “Asynchronous execution” and “CUDA Graphs”; Alan Gray, NVIDIA, [“Getting Started with CUDA Graphs”](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/cuda-graphs/) (2019), measured launch/launch-and-synchronization overhead in a V100 example; Jason Ansel et al., [“PyTorch 2: Faster Machine Learning Through Dynamic Python Bytecode Transformation and Graph Compilation”](https://pytorch.org/assets/pytorch2-2.pdf), *ASPLOS 2024*. “A few microseconds” is an order of magnitude for host-side launch cost; it varies with hardware, driver and framework.

notes.evidence_checked: Dao et al. primary abstract checked: I/O-aware exact attention, tiling, 3× GPT-2 training at sequence 1K versus reported baseline. Bias/ReLU traffic independently calculated: two 2-byte reads and two writes = 8 bytes; two operations / 8 = 0.25. Large-tensor and speedup qualifications added.
notes.citation_and_locator: Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra and Christopher Ré, [“FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135), *NeurIPS 2022*, abstract and §4: exact attention computed in on-chip tiles, with up to about 3× faster GPT-2 training at sequence length 1K against the baseline implementation reported there. The bias-and-activation estimate is illustrative arithmetic: 2 operations per 8 bytes is 0.25 operations per byte, far below the ≈584 operations per byte ridge computed in Interlude 3 for dense FP8 Tensor Core work, and also below the much lower ridge of the general-purpose units that perform elementwise operations; small bias reads are ignored. The roofline figure uses the same two specifications.

notes.evidence_checked: Kaplan et al. primary PDF pp. 5–6, §2.1/Table 1 checked: dominant nonembedding matrix computation ≈2N forward and ≈6N training per token. Context-dependent attention, embeddings and rematerialization are not included in the simple estimate.
notes.citation_and_locator: Jared Kaplan et al., [“Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361) (2020), §2.1, estimating training compute as about $6N$ operations per token for a dense transformer, forward plus backward. The approximation omits embedding and context-length-dependent attention terms and does not apply directly to sparse mixture-of-experts models, where $N$ should be the parameters active per token.

notes.evidence_checked: Meta primary full-text HTML v3 intro and §3.3/Table 4 read: 405B, 15.6T tokens, 3.8e25 FLOPs; 16,384 H100s at 41% MFU for 8K and 38% for 131K. PaLM primary HTML v5 Appendix B read: MFU excludes rematerialization; hardware FLOPs utilization is different. Independent 6ND calculation matches the reported order.
notes.citation_and_locator: Llama Team, AI @ Meta, [“The Llama 3 Herd of Models”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783) (2024), §3 (pretraining on about 15.6 trillion tokens, 3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs for the 405B model) and §3.3 (up to 16,000 H100 GPUs, BF16 model FLOPs utilization of roughly 38–43 percent). Model FLOPs utilization was introduced by Aakanksha Chowdhery et al., [“PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.02311) (2022), Appendix B: MFU counts the model’s useful forward/backward work and excludes rematerialization, unlike hardware FLOPs utilization. Llama 3 Table 4 reports 41% at 8K context and 38% at 131,072 tokens on 16,384 H100s; 43% is the smaller 8,192-GPU run.

notes.evidence_checked: ZeRO primary HTML v3 §3.1–3.2 read: 2-byte weights + 2-byte gradients + 12-byte master/moments = 16 bytes. Mixed Precision Training primary abstract read for FP32 master copy, FP16 weights/gradients and loss scaling. 405B ×16 /180GB =36 is arithmetic before overhead, not a claim Meta trained on B200s.
notes.citation_and_locator: Samyam Rajbhandari, Jeff Rasley, Olatunji Ruwase and Yuxiong He, [“ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models”](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054), *SC20*, §3.1: mixed-precision Adam holds about $16\Psi$ bytes for $\Psi$ parameters; Paulius Micikevicius et al., [“Mixed Precision Training”](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03740), *ICLR 2018*, on the 32-bit master copy. Configurations vary: 8-bit optimizer states, other optimizers and sharding change the total per GPU. The 6.5 TB and thirty-six-GPU figures use decimal bytes: $405\times10^9\times16=6.48\times10^{12}$. Dividing by the B200’s 180 GB gives 36 devices before activations, buffers and other overhead. This is an illustration, not Meta’s actual H100 training layout. The serving bars exclude scale metadata and runtime storage.

notes.evidence_checked: Chen et al. primary abstract read: sublinear-memory training and approximately an extra forward pass. One forward ≈2N / standard train ≈6N =1/3. Selective policies differ.

notes.evidence_checked: Reused this date’s Interlude 3 primary-source check: Williams et al. 2009 pp. 66–67, NVIDIA DGX data sheet p. 8, Blackwell tuning guide. Recomputed dense roof (9 sparse /2 =4.5 PFLOP/s), bandwidth 7.7TB/s, ridge 584.4 ops/byte, weights-only 110 passes/s. Original SVG coordinates and labels inspected; render checked. Not an application benchmark.
notes.citation_and_locator: Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman and David Patterson, [“Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures”](https://aiichironakano.github.io/cs596/Williams-Roofline-CACM09.pdf), *Communications of the ACM* 52(4) (2009), 65–76. The B200 illustration uses [NVIDIA’s DGX data sheet](https://dam-cdn.nvd.orangelogic.com/AssetLink/y441155802qub41q118b2852i557jem5.pdf), p. 8: 7.7 TB/s HBM bandwidth and half the 9 PFLOP/s sparse FP8 rating, or 4.5 PFLOP/s dense. Their ratio is about 584 operations/byte. The [Blackwell tuning guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/blackwell-tuning-guide/index.html) specifies 180 GB usable memory. At 70 GB per dense-model weight pass, 7.7 TB/s gives about 110 passes/s, assuming conventional one-token decoding on one GPU. Cache traffic, other operations and overhead lower the rate; batching, multiple GPUs and speculative decoding change the premise. Prefill processes prompt tokens in parallel but may be chunked. These are idealized ceilings, not measured application speeds.

notes.evidence_checked: Official USENIX authors’ abstract read for iteration-level scheduling, dynamic batching and heterogeneous requests. Batch count and throughput examples independently calculated, not presented as measured Orca performance.
notes.citation_and_locator: Gyeong-In Yu, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim and Byung-Gon Chun, [“Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models”](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu), *OSDI 2022*, on iteration-level scheduling. Sixty-four tokens per pass is an idealization that holds only while arithmetic and cache memory keep up.

notes.evidence_checked: Meta primary Table 3 checked: Llama 3 70B has 80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dimensions/head. 2×80×8×128×2 =327680 bytes/token; ×32000 =10.48576 decimal GB. No inference-memory equivalence to raw weight size.
notes.citation_and_locator: Per-token cache size is $2 \times$ layers $\times$ key-value heads $\times$ head dimension $\times$ bytes per value. For Llama 3 70B (80 layers, 8 key-value heads with grouped-query attention, head dimension 128; Llama Team, “The Llama 3 Herd of Models,” Table 3) at 2 bytes, that is 327,680 bytes per token, or about 10.5 GB for 32,000 tokens. Cache quantization and other architectures change the figure.

notes.evidence_checked: Leviathan et al. primary HTML v2 algorithm 1 and Appendix A.1 read: accept min(1,p/q), rejection from normalized positive p−q, target marginal preserved. Abstract reports 2–3× T5-XXL experiment. Chen et al. primary bibliographic record checked as parallel work; not a claim its full text was read.
notes.citation_and_locator: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman and Yossi Matias, [“Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192), *ICML 2023*, reporting 2–3× acceleration on T5-XXL with identical output distributions; Charlie Chen et al., [“Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01318) (2023). For target probabilities $p$ and draft probabilities $q$, algorithm 1 accepts a proposed token with probability $\min(1,p/q)$; on rejection it samples from the normalized positive part of $p-q$. This preserves the target distribution, not a prespecified identical random sample. Gains depend on draft acceptance and hardware.

inherited_evidence.claim: Logical entropy, exported heat and total production differ
inherited_evidence.evidence_checked: Sagawa 2014 primary full-text §§4 and 5.4 inspected. Physical distinctions do not derive the following managed-continuity hypothesis.
inherited_evidence.citation_and_locator: Takahiro Sagawa, [“Thermodynamic and Logical Reversibilities Revisited”](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.1886), *Journal of Statistical Mechanics*, P03025 (2014), §§4–5. Heat flow to a reservoir, logical entropy change and total entropy production are distinct. The subsequent proposal about managed continuity and agency is an open authorial inquiry, not a result of thermodynamics or an established test for consciousness.
